tencel.origin: TENCEL is a trademark of Lenzing AG of Austria, used as an umbrella brand for more than one generic fiber, chiefly lyocell and modal, so the brand alone does not identify the fiber. Both are regenerated cellulose made from dissolving wood pulp. The lyocell side of the brand descends from the process that Courtaulds of Britain industrialized at Mobile, Alabama; Lenzing acquired the Tencel Group, including the Mobile plant and a plant at Grimsby, England, in 2004.
tencel.structure: Chemically, TENCEL lyocell is cellulose, a linear polymer of glucose units joined by beta-1,4-glycosidic bonds, regenerated in the cellulose II crystal form. Because the polymer is dissolved directly and drawn in an air gap before coagulation, the chains are highly oriented and crystalline, and the fiber is built from long microfibrils lying parallel to its axis. That fibrillar architecture explains both its high wet strength and its tendency to fibrillate: wet abrasion can split fine fibrils from the surface, producing the peach-skin effect that finishers either exploit or suppress. TENCEL modal, by contrast, is made by a modified viscose route and has a different internal structure.
tencel.process: Lenzing describes lyocell production as direct dissolution: wood pulp is mixed with an aqueous solution of N-methylmorpholine N-oxide (NMMO), water is evaporated until the cellulose dissolves into a viscous dope, and the filtered dope is extruded through spinnerets across an air gap into a dilute NMMO bath where the cellulose coagulates (dry-jet wet spinning). The filaments are washed, finished, dried and cut to staple or kept as filament. Lenzing states that more than 99.8% of the solvent is recovered by evaporation and distillation and returned to the loop. No derivative such as cellulose xanthate is formed, which distinguishes this route from viscose.
tencel.performance: Lyocell's regain is roughly 11% at standard conditions, a little lower than viscose because of its higher crystallinity. Published comparisons report lyocell keeping most of its tenacity when wet (in one study roughly 32 cN/tex dry and 29 wet) while viscose loses close to half. Like all cellulose it chars rather than melts, dyes readily with reactive, direct and vat dyes through its hydroxyl groups, and is vulnerable to mildew if stored damp. Fibrillation during wet processing and laundering is the main handling issue; cross-linked grades exist to reduce it. Comfort and sustainability statements on the TENCEL site are the producer's own.
tencel.identify: Burn tests are indicative only and should be done with care: lyocell burns like other cellulose, with a paper-like smell and soft grey ash. Under the microscope it shows a smooth, round to oval cross-section without the serrated outline of standard viscose, and wet abrasion may reveal fibrils. FTIR confirms cellulose but cannot establish the brand. Retail confusion is common: TENCEL can mean lyocell or modal, so the generic name on the label is what identifies the fiber.
tencel.labeling: TENCEL is a trademark, not a generic fiber name. In the United States the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act (15 U.S.C. 70 et seq.) and the FTC rules at 16 CFR Part 303 require the generic name; the FTC added lyocell in 1996 as a recognized subclass of rayon, and a trademark may appear only alongside the generic name. In the EU, Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 requires the listed fiber name (lyocell or modal). Any certification a product carries should be checked on the certificate itself rather than inferred from the brand.
tencel.past: Solvent spinning of cellulose in amine oxides was developed as an alternative to the viscose route, and Courtaulds brought it to commercial scale under the Tencel name at Mobile, Alabama, reaching full production in the early 1990s. Courtaulds petitioned the FTC in 1992 for a new generic name, received a temporary designation so the fiber need not be called rayon, and saw lyocell formally adopted in 1996. Lenzing, a former competitor, acquired the Tencel Group in 2004, combining the brand with its own lyocell and modal output. The brand later became Lenzing's main textile umbrella for specialty cellulosics.

ecovero.origin: LENZING ECOVERO is a viscose fiber brand of Lenzing AG, launched in 2017. The generic fiber is viscose (called rayon in the United States), a regenerated cellulose spun from dissolving wood pulp. Lenzing states that the wood comes from forests certified under FSC or PEFC chain-of-custody systems. The brand differentiates a commodity fiber type through sourcing, process-emission claims and traceability documentation rather than through a new chemistry.
ecovero.structure: ECOVERO fiber is chemically the same as other viscose: cellulose regenerated as the cellulose II polymorph, with glucose units linked by beta-1,4 bonds and a degree of polymerization lower than in cotton. The viscose process typically gives a skin-core morphology and an irregular, lobed or serrated cross-section formed as the filament shrinks during coagulation. Crystallinity and orientation are lower than in lyocell, which is why viscose absorbs more water, swells more, and loses much of its strength when wet. The brand name does not describe a distinct molecular structure.
ecovero.process: In the viscose route that ECOVERO follows, pulp is steeped in sodium hydroxide to form alkali cellulose, aged, then reacted with carbon disulfide to form cellulose xanthate (xanthation). The xanthate dissolves in dilute alkali to give the viscose dope, which is ripened, filtered and extruded into an acid bath of sulfuric acid and salts, where the cellulose regenerates and the sulfur compounds are released. Lenzing states that ECOVERO production meets EU Ecolabel criteria and uses at least 50% less water and generates about half the carbon emissions of generic viscose; those comparisons are producer claims tied to its own chosen baseline.
ecovero.performance: In use ECOVERO behaves like good-quality viscose: high moisture uptake, soft drape and bright dye uptake with reactive and direct dyes, which bind to cellulose hydroxyl groups. Wet strength is its weak point; published comparisons show viscose losing close to half its tenacity when wet, so wet agitation and wringing can distort fabrics. It chars rather than melts, is not thermoplastic and cannot be heat-set like polyester. Shrinkage and creasing depend heavily on finishing. Biodegradability and lower-impact statements come from Lenzing and apply to defined products and test conditions.
ecovero.identify: Burn tests are indicative only: viscose burns quickly with an afterglow, a burning-paper smell and little ash. Microscopy shows longitudinal striations and a serrated cross-section typical of viscose. No routine lab method distinguishes ECOVERO from other viscose, because the polymer is the same. Verifying the brand therefore depends on supply-chain documents, license numbers and producer confirmation rather than on the fiber itself.
ecovero.labeling: ECOVERO is a trademark, not a generic name. US labels must say rayon or viscose under the TFPIA and 16 CFR Part 303, and EU labels must use viscose under Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011, with the brand shown only in addition. Lenzing reports that ECOVERO holds the EU Ecolabel for textile products (license AT/016/001) and that its wood is FSC or PEFC certified. Those are claims about specific certificates; brands should check that the certificate scope covers the product being sold.
ecovero.past: Viscose rayon has been produced industrially since the early twentieth century, and its reputation has long been shaped by carbon disulfide emissions, wastewater and forest sourcing. Lenzing launched ECOVERO in 2017 as a branded response to those concerns, reporting that it was the first viscose to carry the EU Ecolabel at launch. The brand was later extended to products using Lenzing's REFIBRA recycled-cotton technology. Its history illustrates a broader trend: distinguishing a commodity fiber by audited process data and certification instead of by chemistry.
facts: at least 50% less water and about half the carbon emissions of generic viscose
